# Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

## The Traditional View of Toughness

When college students were asked to describe toughness, words like hard-nosed, gritty, playing through pain, stoic, and persevering came to mind. Among 160 elite athletes, perseverance ranked highest. The conventional image is a football player popping a dislocated shoulder back in, or Craig MacTavish (last NHL player without a helmet, retired 1997). Toughness is traditionally seen as overcoming obstacles through perseverance, discipline, and stoicism—often pictured as a strong brute of a man.

## Bobby Knight’s Model

Bobby Knight won over 900 games (third all-time), three NCAA championships, and a perfect 1976 season. He defined toughness as “being able to overcome obstacles. You can’t feel sorry for yourself.” His 1976 team pioneered a pressing man-to-man defense. But his methods included: tampons hung in lockers of “soft” players, accusations of taping pictures of women’s genitalia in players’ rooms, a 1991 tirade (“This is absolute fucking bullshit… I’ll fucking run your ass right into the ground”), bringing toilet paper with shit to show players what he thought of them, and choking a player on video. His definition of toughness was founded on showing no weakness, bulldozing obstacles, and using fear to establish authority.

## Tough Parenting

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind (1960s) classified parenting styles by two factors: **responsiveness** (attunement, support, fostering individuality) and **demandingness** (expectations, control, discipline). Three categories emerged:
- **Permissive**: low demandingness, high responsiveness (too soft)
- **Authoritarian**: high demandingness, low responsiveness (too hard)
- **Authoritative**: high demandingness, high responsiveness (Goldilocks fit)

Authoritarian parents rely on fear, threats, punishment (“because I said so”). In one study of over 1,000 parents, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should “love their child unconditionally.” Another study found 81% of Americans thought parents were too soft on children. The problem is not punishment or expectations per se, but when demandingness far outweighs support. The same principle applies to coaching and leadership: we’ve taken the demanding part and forgotten warmth, care, and responsiveness.

## Callousness as Fake Toughness

The language of toughness equates it with callousness: “soft,” “hardening up,” “show no signs of weakness.” In youth sports, children are made to run laps or do burpees to “toughen them up.” Mark Hyman’s *Until It Hurts* documented frequent vomiting after workouts and insult-laden tirades, justified by parents as necessary for children “to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior.” Toughness has been tied to masculinity and machismo: “man up,” “stop being a pussy,” “There’s no crying in baseball!” (from *A League of Their Own*). The archetype is The Rock or Vin Diesel—brute strength with bravado. Yet women, who research shows handle pain better than men, may have had the correct definition all along.

## The Downfall of Callous Toughness

On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair, 19, showed signs of profound fatigue during ten 110-yard sprints. Coaches and trainers yelled “get him the [expletive] up” and “drag his [expletive] across the field.” After his final sprint, it took trainers 34 minutes to get him off the field and another 28 minutes to call 911. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke. A rash of player deaths and injuries from extreme workouts has occurred, including rhabdomyolysis (damaged muscle products leaking into bloodstream). Ohio University professor B. David Ridpath noted these workouts are designed “to either toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots.”

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggression, higher substance abuse and risky behaviors. In sport, it’s linked to lower grit, increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, and fear of failure. In a study of over 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting was linked to higher child misbehavior. In the Israeli military, those from authoritarian environments coped worse with military life. One young athlete explained punishment-based motivation: “Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger… I need to work harder because I don’t want to be punished.” This creates fragile, dependent individuals who respond only to external fear and control.

## Redefining Toughness

Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, and based on appearance over substance. Real toughness is: “experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.”

Pete Carroll (one of only three coaches to win both NCAA championship and Super Bowl) exemplifies real toughness. He encourages meditation, yoga, and ring toss to defuse tension. He says, “Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they’ve been prepared to do.” His “always compete” practices emphasize inner drive, not fear. Other successful coaches with similar approaches: Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy, John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, Mike D’Antoni (“We keep it positive here”). As Ken Reed summarized, “For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach.”

A 2008 Eastern Washington study of nearly 200 basketball players found that mental toughness does not come from autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive styles, but from “an environment which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service.”

## The Author’s Personal Experience

The author, a University of Houston runner, competed in the Don Bowden Mile (Bowden was first American to break four minutes in 1957). At 900 meters into the 1,609-meter race, he experienced a strange high-pitched gasp and tightening in his neck. His inner voice screamed “I can’t breathe!” He collapsed. After a year of tests, allergist Dr. Stephen Miles diagnosed paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)—the vocal cords shut when they should open, blocking inhalation. The American Thoracic Society cites “strong emotions” and stress as triggers. The author’s old strategy of pushing until he puked backfired. He had to learn to relax and keep his breathing, neck, and mind steady at the moment of maximum discomfort. This search for real toughness became the book.

## The Four Pillars of Real Toughness

1. **Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality**
2. **Listen to Your Body**
3. **Respond Instead of React**
4. **Transcend Discomfort**

The chapter concludes: real toughness isn’t about bulldozing through; it’s about navigating discomfort—sometimes going through, around, under, or waiting until it passes. It requires many tools, not just a hammer.

# Organizing: Setting Up the Right Buckets

## The Basic Categories

Seven primary types to track: Projects list, project support material, calendar actions/information, Next Actions lists, Waiting For list, reference material, Someday/Maybe list.

**Hard edges are critical.** Categories must be kept visually, physically, and psychologically separate. If reference mixes with things to read, you go numb to the stack. If calendar-bound actions stay on action lists, you won't trust your calendar. If inactive projects stay on Projects list, it loses action-generating focus. If Waiting For items mix with action lists, nonproductive rethinking bogs you down.

**All you need are lists and folders.** A "list" can be: (1) a file folder with separate paper notes; (2) a titled paper in a loose-leaf organizer; (3) an inventory in software. Don't impose external priority scaffolding—you'll prioritize intuitively against shifting variables. The list is just a way to track the total inventory of active commitments.

## Organizing Action Reminders

### Calendar Actions
The calendar should show only the "hard landscape"—time-specific ("10:00–11:00 meet with Jim") or day-specific ("Call Rachel Tuesday"). Resist putting actions you'd like to do but might not; the calendar must be sacred territory reflecting exact hard edges. When relegated to its proper role, most actions remain in the "as soon as possible, against all other things I have to do" category.

### As-Soon-As-Possible Actions by Context
Organize by tool, location, or situation required. How discrete categories need to be depends on (1) how many actions you track and (2) how often you change contexts. With 25 next actions, a single list might suffice; with 50–100, you need sorting. This leverages energy when in a certain mode—when in "phone mode," crank down your Calls list; when at a computer, do all digital work at once.

**Most common list headings:**
- **Calls** – all phone calls; record numbers alongside each item. A discrete Calls category makes it easier to use strange little windows of time (waiting for a plane, kid coming out from school).
- **At Computer** – actions requiring a computer. Allen maintains a separate **Online** list for when he's on a plane without Wi-Fi, so he doesn't have to rethink what he can and can't do. If work is mobile-centric, a single Digital context list or Anywhere category might work.
- **Errands** – e.g., "Get stock certificates from bank deposit box," "Pick up suit at the tailor," "Buy flowers for Robyn at the florist." Sublists within items (e.g., "hardware store" with appended items) are useful. Location-based reminders from GPS exist but are still overoptimistic for total trust.
- **At Office** – actions requiring physical presence (e.g., purging a filing cabinet). "Hotel-ing" (no permanent office) is rising; you may need At Office A and B lists for different locations.
- **At Home** – e.g., "Hang new watercolor print," "Organize travel accessories," "Switch closets to winter clothes." If you work only at home, At Home suffices without At Office.
- **Agendas** – separate lists for bosses, partners, assistants, children, standing meetings (staff, board, committee). Add ad hoc as needed—insert a page in a loose-leaf notebook or a note in digital tools. The broader your responsibilities, the more you get things done through communications with others.
- **Read/Review** – longer-than-two-minute reading items best managed in a physical stack tray. Some professionals also use a **Review/Respond** category for more rigorous reading. For digital input, a **Review/Watch** file or **Surf Web** action list can hold links to videos, blogs, or articles.

### Organizing "Waiting For"
Track final deliverables or projects others are responsible for (e.g., tickets ordered, scanner coming, client approval). Include the date requested and any agreed-upon due date—"just this one tactical detail is worth its weight in gold." Keep this list close to Next Actions; responsibility may bounce back and forth many times before a project finishes. Digital list managers let you move items between categories without rewriting. Having this list available when meeting with responsible parties allows early, elegant conversations rather than overdue stress.

### Using the Original Item as Its Own Action Reminder
Some inputs serve best as their own reminders (e.g., magazines in Read/Review tray, bills in "Bills to Pay" folder, receipts in "Receipts to Process" envelope). This approach can be dangerous if you don't put those items in front of your face consistently. For e-mail: create @ACTION and @WAITING FOR folders that sort to the top of the navigator bar. Getting e-mail "in" to empty means deleting, filing, doing <2-minute responses, and moving actionable e-mails into @ACTION. "It takes much less energy to maintain e-mail backlog at zero than at a thousand."

**Caution about dispersing reminders:** If data is offscreen, it can disappear as a viable prompt. Review all categories equally. "You don't want things lurking in the recesses of your systems and not being used for their intended purpose: reminding you." The digital world is dangerous here—offscreen data tends to disappear as a prompt, causing some to revert to paper planners for physical trust.

## Organizing Project Reminders

### The Projects List
A comprehensive index of open loops (every commitment requiring more than one action step). You don't work off it moment-to-moment; its real value is the complete weekly review ensuring action steps exist for all projects. "A complete and current Projects list is the major operational tool for moving from tree-hugging to forest management."

**Value of a complete list:**
- Critical for control and focus – "I've got to get my driver's license renewed" can take up as much mental space as "I need to formulate the agenda for next year's conference."
- Alleviates subtle tensions – small things slip into bigger ones (registration forms, invoice disputes). Getting these identified creates fresh energy.
- Core of the Weekly Review – marrying larger commitments to day-to-day activities.
- Facilitates relationship management – triggers important conversations about commitments with bosses, staff, partners, family.

**Where to find hidden projects:**
1. **Current activities** – calendar meetings, next actions, proposals/contracts in briefcase. Example: "Call Mario re: the fund-raising event" on Calls list but "Finalize the fund-raiser" not yet on Projects list.
2. **Higher-horizon interests** – professional accountabilities, goals, strategic plans, personal life (kids, retirement, partner's aspirations). Reviewing long-range planning documents almost always reveals at least one unclarified project.
3. **Current problems, issues, opportunities** – problems (always projects), process improvements, creative/capacity-building opportunities. Examples: "Look into improving Frederick's relationship with his school," "Resolve situation with landlord and building maintenance," "Get closure on compensation dispute with business partner."

**One list or subdivided?** Most find one list best as a master inventory. Common subsorts: personal/professional, delegated projects, specific types (e.g., "Projects—Presentations" for a speaker). "The right amount of complexity is whatever creates optimal simplicity." How you group is less critical than ensuring the inventory is complete, current, and assessed sufficiently.

**Subprojects:** If big pieces depend on others, list the major project and keep subpieces in support material. If independent, list separately. Allen's example: "Move to Amsterdam" was one project; later unpacked into fifteen (e.g., "Set up Dutch bank accounts," "Finalize artwork storage in Santa Barbara").

### Project Support Materials
Resources to support actions and thinking—not reminders. Don't use support material for reminding; that creates "an incessant subliminal chant: 'Do something about me!'" First add the project to Projects list, put action steps on appropriate lists, then pull support materials when doing the action. If materials contain project plans and overviews, store them visibly accessible for Weekly Review.

**Organizing ad hoc project thinking:**
- **Attached notes** – in software or Post-it on paper list.
- **Email/software** – dedicated reference folders; consider "Active" and "Archive" folders per project. "The inherent danger in the digital world is how much data can be spread into how many different places so easily, without coordinating links."
- **Paper-based files** – separate folder per project; often easier for planning sessions. Allen prints spreadsheets, schedules, e-mails, Web pages for physical reference.
- **Pages in notebooks** – loose-leaf allows dedicated pages per project. Allen maintained a midsize notebook with Projects list in front and Project Support section toward back.

## Organizing Nonactionable Data

### Reference Materials
Once you've distinguished actionable from nonactionable, reference has no pull—it's just your library. "If material is purely for reference, the only issue is whether it's worth the time and space to keep it." As Allen increased hard disk space and cloud backup, he kept more e-mail archives and digital photos—"the more the merrier."

**Variety of reference systems:**
- **General-reference filing** – paper, email, simple digital storage. Need 1–4 physical file drawers, dozens of email folders. Allen tracks restaurants worldwide in a software application with hundreds of folders and subfolders.
- **Large-category filing** – topics requiring >50 folders get their own section/drawer/database (e.g., corporate merger due-diligence cabinets). Best to stick with one general-reference system except for very limited discrete topics.
- **Contact managers** – purely reference; don't use for action reminders unless part of a well-functioning CRM. Many people have stacks of business cards subtly yelling "Decide something about me!"
- **Libraries and archives** – personalized levels: always-with-you mobile device, briefcase, office filing, off-site storage, cloud. "There is no 'perfect' reference system." Start with real information, decide best place for retrievability, craft from the ground up.

### Someday/Maybes
Track things to reassess in the future. "Someday/Maybes are not throwaway items. They may be some of the most interesting and creative things you'll ever get involved with."

**Someday/Maybe list** – e.g., "Learn Spanish," "Get Marcie a horse," "Climb Mt. Washington," "Write a mystery novel," "Get a vacation cottage." Allen's experience: learning flute and sailing started here. Sources: creative imagination and current projects. Subcategorize if helpful (e.g., home projects vs. bucket list). Pay attention to whether subcategories are unnerving or energizing.

**Special categories:** Food (recipes, restaurants), children's activities, books to read, music to download, movies, gift ideas, weekend trips, miscellaneous ideas. These are cross between reference and Someday/Maybe.

**Danger of "Hold and Review" files:** "In virtually every case I have come across, the person held but didn't review." After processing, often nothing left—much needs tossing, some goes to Read/Review, some to reference, some to calendar or tickler, some has actual next actions.

**Using the calendar for future options:**
- Triggers for activating projects (e.g., annual sales conference, kids' school setup, birthdays/anniversaries).
- Events you might want to participate in (seminars, conferences).
- Decision catalysts – "It's OK to decide not to decide—as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system." Major decisions: hire/fire, merge/acquire, change job/career, strategy redirection. Use "private" categorization for group-accessible calendars.

**Tickler file:** 43 folders – 31 daily ("1"–"31") and 12 monthly. Daily files in front starting with tomorrow's date; emptied into in-tray each day and refiled at back. Monthly files emptied when they reach front and refiled a year ahead. Allows storing actual documents (forms, agendas, invoices). Must check and update every day. If you leave town, check folders for days you'll be away before you go.

## Checklists: Creative and Constructive Reminders

Alfred North Whitehead: "Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them." Checklists provide that micro version.

**Things you want to pay attention to** – fuzzy commitments like "Exercise more regularly," "Maintain good morale on my team." First identify inherent projects and actions (e.g., "Set up regular exercise program" + "Call Sally about gyms"). For things that don't fit, use overview checklists.

**Blueprinting key areas** – multiple levels of outcomes and standards: career goals, service, family, relationships, community, health, financial resources, creative expression. Within a job: team morale, processes, timelines, staff issues, workload, communications, technology. Often the value is simply affirming the area is OK as is.

**More novel situation, more control required** – if you've been doing something a long time, minimal external organization needed. New responsibilities (e.g., suddenly filling CEO's shoes, new position) require checklists until automatic. Allen used checklists for accounting, computers, marketing, legal, administration when restructuring a business. He is "dangerously semiliterate" with computers and creates checklists for recurring IT fixes.

**Checklists at all levels** – from "Core Life Values" to "Things to Take Camping" to "Potential Holiday Gifts." Examples: Job Areas of Responsibility, Exercise Regimens, Travel Checklist, Weekly Review, Training Program Components, Key Clients, People to Stay in Touch With, Year-end Activities, Personal Development, Jokes. "Capability and willingness to instantly make a checklist, accessible and used when needed, is a core component of high-performance self-management."

Resources to support actions and thinking—not reminders. Don't use support material for reminding; that creates "an incessant subliminal chant: 'Do something about me!'" First add the project to Projects list, put action steps on appropriate lists, then pull support materials when doing the action.

**Organizing ad hoc project thinking:**
- **Attached notes** – in software or Post-it on paper list.
- **Email/software** – dedicated reference folders; consider "Active" and "Archive" folders per project. "The inherent danger in the digital world is how much data can be spread into how many different places so easily, without coordinating links."
- **Paper-based files** – separate folder per project; often easier for planning sessions.
- **Pages in notebooks** – loose-leaf allows dedicated pages per project.

## Organizing Nonactionable Data

### Reference Materials
Once you've distinguished actionable from nonactionable, reference has no pull—it's just your library. "If material is purely for reference, the only issue is whether it's worth the time and space to keep it."

**Variety of reference systems:**
- **General-reference filing** – paper, email, simple digital storage. Need 1–4 physical file drawers, dozens of email folders.
- **Large-category filing** – topics requiring >50 folders get their own section/drawer/database (e.g., corporate merger due-diligence cabinets).
- **Contact managers** – purely reference; don't use for action reminders unless part of a well-functioning CRM.
- **Libraries and archives** – personalized levels: always-with-you mobile device, briefcase, office filing, off-site storage, cloud. "There is no 'perfect' reference system."

### Someday/Maybes
Track things to reassess in the future. "Someday/Maybes are not throwaway items. They may be some of the most interesting and creative things you'll ever get involved with."

**Someday/Maybe list** – e.g., "Learn Spanish," "Get Marcie a horse," "Climb Mt. Washington," "Write a mystery novel," "Get a vacation cottage." Allen's experience: learning flute and sailing started here. Sources: creative imagination and current projects. Subcategorize if helpful (e.g., home projects vs. bucket list).

**Special categories:** Food (recipes, restaurants), children's activities, books to read, music to download, movies, gift ideas, weekend trips, miscellaneous ideas.

**Danger of "Hold and Review" files:** "In virtually every case I have come across, the person held but didn't review." After processing, often nothing left.

**Using the calendar for future options:**
- Triggers for activating projects (e.g., annual sales conference, kids' school setup).
- Events you might want to participate in (seminars, conferences).
- Decision catalysts – "It's OK to decide not to decide—as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system." Major decisions: hire/fire, merge/acquire, change job/career, strategy redirection.

**Tickler file:** 43 folders – 31 daily ("1"–"31") and 12 monthly. Daily files in front starting with tomorrow's date; emptied into in-tray each day and refiled at back. Monthly files emptied when they reach front and refiled a year ahead. Allows storing actual documents (forms, agendas, invoices). Must check and update every day.

## Checklists: Creative and Constructive Reminders

Alfred North Whitehead: "Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them." Checklists provide that micro version.

**Things you want to pay attention to** – fuzzy commitments like "Exercise more regularly," "Maintain good morale on my team." First identify inherent projects and actions (e.g., "Set up regular exercise program" + "Call Sally about gyms"). For things that don't fit, use overview checklists.

**Blueprinting key areas** – multiple levels of outcomes and standards: career goals, service, family, relationships, community, health, financial resources, creative expression. Within a job: team morale, processes, timelines, staff issues, workload, communications, technology.

**More novel situation, more control required** – if you've been doing something a long time, minimal external organization needed. New responsibilities (e.g., suddenly filling CEO's shoes, new position) require checklists until automatic. Allen used checklists for accounting, computers, marketing, legal, administration when restructuring a business.

**Checklists at all levels** – from "Core Life Values" to "Things to Take Camping" to "Potential Holiday Gifts." Examples: Job Areas of Responsibility, Exercise Regimens, Travel Checklist, Weekly Review, Training Program Components, Key Clients, People to Stay in Touch With, Year-end Activities, Personal Development, Jokes. "Capability and willingness to instantly make a checklist, accessible and used when needed, is a core component of high-performance self-management."

It effectively conveys the critical qualifiers about the need for a better physical organization system than a mental one and the evolving nature of organization. However, it slightly underrepresents the nuances of how to manage specific categories and the importance of context in organizing actions. The structure is clear and coherent, making it easy to follow.
